title: Bisque de homard
subtitle: Classic French lobster bisque
excerpt: Rich, velvet-smooth cream soup built from lobster shells, aromatic vegetables, brandy, and cream. A classic of French restaurant cookery, and the most labour-intensive of the bisque family.
sourceNotes: Bisque de homard appears in Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire (1903) and in Louis Saulnier's Le Répertoire de la Cuisine (1914), both widely available as public-domain or historical culinary reference works. The technique of roasting crustacean shells to build a bisque base is a core French classical method.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze before adding the cream. Defrost, reheat gently, then add the cream to finish.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The base (without cream) can be made 2 days ahead and refrigerated. Add cream and finish just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A smooth, rich, cream-based soup made from the roasted shells of crustaceans such as lobster, crab, or prawn. The shells are cooked with vegetables and aromatics, the liquid is strained and reduced, then finished with cream.

content.text: is a two-stage soup. First, roast and simmer the shells with vegetables, wine, and brandy to draw out every bit of flavour. Then strain, reduce, and finish with cream. The result is rich and velvety. It takes some time, but it is the right thing for a special occasion.

items.prepNote: cooked, meat removed and reserved; shells and heads kept

content.text: Heat the oven to 180°C. Arrange the lobster shells and heads on a roasting tray and roast for 15 minutes until they smell fragrant and are starting to colour. This step deepens the flavour significantly.
Heat a splash of oil in a large, heavy pan over high heat. Add the roasted shells and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes. Add the onion, carrot, and celery and cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally.

Add the tomato purée and stir it in. Pour in the brandy and let it bubble and reduce by half. Add the white wine and reduce by half again. Pour in the fish stock and bring to the boil. Simmer for 40 minutes.
Strain the stock through a fine sieve into a clean saucepan, pressing hard on the shells to extract all the liquid. Discard the solids. Bring the strained liquid to the boil and reduce by one third.
Add the double cream and simmer gently for 5 minutes. Whisk in the butter in small pieces. Season with salt and a pinch of cayenne.
Cut the reserved lobster meat into chunks and add to the bisque to warm through. Serve immediately in warm bowls.

items.symptom: Bisque tastes thin and lacks depth
items.cause: Shells not roasted, or stock not reduced enough
items.fix: Never skip the roasting step. Reduce the strained liquid more aggressively before adding cream.

items.cause: Cream added to a boiling liquid and split
items.fix: Add cream to a gently simmering bisque, not a boiling one. If it has split, blend briefly and strain again.

content.text: Bisque de homard is a hallmark of French classical restaurant cooking. It appears on menus from Normandy and Brittany, where the lobsters come from, to the grand dining rooms of Paris. At home it is a dish for occasions: the shells from two lobsters are the minimum to get enough depth of flavour, which means you are also dealing with the lobster meat as a main course or as the garnish in the bisque itself. Both are right.
